title: White wine, dyed red, got red-wine words

angle.point: A glass of white wine isn't boring: dye it red and trained wine students describe its smell with the words they use for red wine, because what they see overrides what they smell.
angle.stakes: Frédéric Brochet, a doctoral researcher at Bordeaux's Faculty of Oenology, was working towards his doctorate on how much of a taster's words come from the wine itself, and his team's test could show they come from its colour instead.
angle.turn: A week after the students described a real red and a real white, Brochet's team gave them the same white wine twice, one glass dyed red with a pigment checked to have no smell, and they generally gave the dyed glass their red-wine words.
angle.takeaway: The words wine tasters use for a smell can come from the colour they see, shown with one odourless dye and the same white wine in two glasses.

beats.speaker: blink
beats.voiceover: White wine, dyed red, got red-wine words.

beats.speaker: blink
beats.voiceover: Wine researcher Frédéric Brochet's team suspected a wine's colour steers which smells tasters name.

elements.text: Does colour steer the smell words?

beats.speaker: blink
beats.voiceover: So they dyed a white wine red with grape pigment, checked to have no smell. Wine students wrote smell words for a real red and white. A week later, Brochet's team gave them the white twice, one glass dyed.

beats.speaker: blink
beats.voiceover: They generally gave the dyed glass their red-wine words. The dye had no smell, so their eyes overruled their noses.

beats.speaker: blink
beats.voiceover: Their 2001 paper called it a real perceptual illusion.

claims.claim: Part of a white wine was dyed red, and tasters generally described the dyed white with the smell words they had used for a red wine.
claims.note: Dossier f11 and f25. "Got red-wine words" = the students generally used the descriptors they had used for wine R to describe wine RW. They were not asked the wine's colour.

claims.claim: Frédéric Brochet was a researcher at the Faculty of Oenology in Bordeaux and a co-author of the study.
claims.note: Dossier f3. "Brochet's team" = the three authors Gil Morrot, Frédéric Brochet and Denis Dubourdieu; Morrot is first author. Brochet did the work towards a doctorate (f4).

claims.claim: The researchers suspected that a wine's colour directs how its smell is identified.
claims.note: Dossier f8: "initially led us to hypothesize that the color of a wine directs the identification of its odor." On screen as a question: "Does colour steer the smell words?"

claims.claim: Part of the white wine was dyed red with purified grape anthocyanins, the red pigment of grapes.
claims.note: Dossier f11 (2 g/L of purified grape anthocyanins). Also on screen: "Dye — Grape pigment, no smell".

claims.claim: The dye was checked to have no smell: 50 people compared the dyed and plain white wine and found them identical.
claims.note: Dossier f12 and f13. The paper reports the odour check only, not a taste check.

claims.claim: Oenology students wrote lists of smell words for a real red wine and a real white wine in the first session.
claims.note: Dossier f14 and f17: 54 undergraduates from the Faculty of Oenology of the University of Bordeaux. On screen: "Session 1 — Real red, real white".

claims.claim: One week later, in the second session, the two wines were the white wine and the same white wine dyed red.
claims.note: Dossier f15 and f23. On screen: "A week later — White, dyed white"; on the twist, the two glasses are labelled "Same white wine".

claims.claim: In the second session the students generally used the smell words they had used for the red wine to describe the dyed white wine.
claims.note: Dossier f25: "generally". The paper gives no count of how many did.

claims.claim: Because the dye had no smell, the authors conclude that, because of what they saw, the tasters discounted what they smelled.
claims.note: Dossier f13 and f27: "because of the visual information, the tasters discounted the olfactory information." Said as "their eyes overruled their noses".

claims.claim: The study, "The Color of Odors", was published in Brain and Language in 2001.
claims.note: Dossier f1. 2001 is the publication year, not the year of the tastings. On screen: "The Color of Odors 2001".

claims.claim: The authors call the effect a real perceptual illusion.
claims.note: Dossier f28: "The observed phenomenon is a real perceptual illusion."

publish.title: White wine, dyed red, got red-wine words
publish.description: Bordeaux wine students described a white wine and a red. A week later they got the same white twice, one glass dyed red with a grape pigment that has no smell, and generally gave it their red-wine words. From "The Color of Odors" (Brain and Language, 2001).
